subject: Different color of geom_line for different values

messages.author: df7df0b1d4b663ae
messages.subject: Different color of geom_line for different values
parts:
I would like a line on a graph to be a different color at different
values.

#Dummy code:
year <- 1900:1999
value <- runif(100, -2, 2)
mydata <- data.frame(year=year, value=value)
p <- ggplot() + geom_line(data=mydata, aes(x=year, y=value))
p

Could someone suggest a straightforward way to make the line blue if
it is a positive value (plotted north of a hypothetical "0" hline) and
red if it is a negative value (south of the hline)?

Alternatively (and better yet), is there a straightforward way to
shade the area between the geom_line and a hypothetical "0" hline such
that years with positive values would be shaded blue and years with
negative values shaded red?

Many, many, thanks.

James

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Different color of geom_line for different values
parts:
Hi:

How about this:

p + geom_ribbon(aes(x = year, ymin = 0, ymax = value * (value > 0)),
fill = alpha('blue', 0.3)) +
geom_ribbon(aes(x = year, ymax = 0, ymin = value * (value < 0)),
fill = alpha('red', 0.3))

HTH,
Dennis

Dennis, this is precisely the guidance I needed. Thanks very much.
It's cool how functional the geoms are with a little tweaking. The
problem is the right tweaks don't occur to me...

My graphic is shaping up nicely, but there's a few more tweaks that I
can't for the life of me figure out how to accomplish. If you're
willing to offer a little more help, I'd appreciate it.

Some dummy code:

my.data <- data.frame(year=year, value=value)
hist.years <- c(1910, 1910, 1930, 1930, 1940, 1980, 1980)
hist.data <- data.frame(hist.years=hist.years)
line <- c(1,-2,-2,2,1,-1)
line.years <-c(1900, 1920, 1940, 1950, 1960, 1990)
line.data <- data.frame(line.years=line.years, line=line)
p <- ggplot() + geom_ribbon(aes(x = year, ymin = 0, ymax = value *
(value > 0), fill="Warm")) + geom_ribbon(aes(x = year, ymax = 0, ymin
= value * (value < 0), fill="Cool")) + geom_histogram(data=hist.data,
aes(x=hist.years, fill="Histogram")) + scale_fill_manual(name="",
c("Warm"='red', "Cool"='blue', "Histogram"='black'))
p + scale_y_continuous(limits=c(-4,4)) + geom_line(data=line.data,
aes(x=line.years, y=line, color="Line")) + scale_color_manual(name="",
c("Line"='darkgreen'))

Two issues:

First, I would like the histogram to appear at the bottom of the plot,
with the floor at around the -4 y coordinate. I want it to appear
below and out of the way of the the other three objects (the two
ribbons and the line).

A related issue to this first issue is that it would be nice to have
two y-scales, one for the ribbons (which in the real graphic are a
temperature series in standard deviation units) and one for the
histogram that I want to sit below it (which is just counts).

Second, I would like the four legend elements to be nested close
together. I don't want the "Line" element to be all by itself.

I sure appreciate any help. As you may see with my dummy code, I'm
not sure I'm hip to the most efficient strategies for mapping between
objects and the legend.

Thanks again,

James

P.S. I'd send a copy of the actual graphic I'm working on, but can't
figure out how to attach with this interface. I can send via
email.

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Different color of geom_line for different values
parts:
Hi:

You can get part of what you want, but the double y-scale thing ain't
happening - it's a design feature, not a bug.

Try this:

library('ggplot2')
my.data <- data.frame(year = 1900:1999, value = runif(100, -2, 2))

# count() is a function in the plyr package
# to compute frequencies quickly:
hist.data <- count(hist.years)
line.data <- data.frame(line.years = c(1900, 1920, 1940, 1950, 1960, 1990),
line = c(1,-2,-2,2,1,-1))

ggplot(my.data) +

geom_ribbon(aes(x = year, ymin = 0,
ymax = value * (value > 0), fill="Warm")) +
geom_ribbon(aes(x = year, ymax = 0,
ymin = value * (value < 0), fill="Cool")) +

geom_segment(data=hist.data, aes(x = x, xend = x,
y = -4, yend = -4 + freq, fill="Histogram"),
size = 3) +
geom_line(data = line.data, aes(x = line.years, y = line,
fill = 'Line'),
size = 1) +
scale_fill_manual(name="",
values = c("Warm"='red', "Cool"='blue',
"Histogram"='black',
"Line" = 'darkgreen')) +
scale_y_continuous(limits=c(-4, 4))

I have to say I'm concerned about all of these features in one plot -
think of the term 'mixed metaphors' and apply it to this graphic. It
'works' only to the extent that none of the elements overlap except
the line, which I presume is somehow related to the time series. If
the counts were larger, the histogram would start encroaching on the
time plot. It might be better to separate the histogram into another
graph, say below the main one that takes up about 20% of the graphics
space on a page, to which you could impose an independent y-scale. One
consequence would be that the histogram label in the legend would no
longer apply, but that seems a minor quibble.

There are several ways to combine two or more independent graphs on a
single graphics page. One approach is outlined at the end of Chapter 8
in Hadley's ggplot2 book using the grid package and viewports. Here's
an example:

mdata <- merge(my.data, hist.data, by.x = 'year', by.y = 'x', all.x = TRUE)
mdata$freq[is.na(mdata$freq)] <- 0

p <- ggplot(my.data) +

geom_ribbon(aes(x = year, ymin = 0,
ymax = value * (value > 0), fill="Warm")) +
geom_ribbon(aes(x = year, ymax = 0,
ymin = value * (value < 0), fill="Cool")) +

geom_line(data = line.data, aes(x = line.years, y = line,
fill = 'Line'),
size = 1) +
scale_fill_manual(name="",
values = c("Warm"='red', "Cool"='blue',
"Line" = 'darkgreen')) +
xlab("") +
opts(legend.position = 'top',
legend.direction = 'horizontal',
axis.text.x = theme_blank(),
axis.title.x = theme_blank())


q <- ggplot(mdata, aes(x = year, y = freq)) +
geom_histogram(stat = 'identity') +
scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:2)

grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(100, 1)))

vplayout <- function(x, y)
viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col = y)

print(p, vp = vplayout(1:75, 1))
print(q, vp = vplayout(73:100, 1))

This is the general idea, but there is an annoying problem: the
horizontal axis in the two plots don't line up even though they use
the same data frame and the same x variable. One can see that the
bottom plot has a shorter horizontal extent than the one above it. I
have no immediate solution to the problem even though I'm probably
missing something obvious. Perhaps someone can offer a fix that aligns
the horizontal scale in both plots, because I don't see it at the
moment.

Dennis
